questions.q: What happens if migrated code keeps using T-SQL's + operator to concatenate strings in MySQL?
options: It either produces an error or silently does arithmetic if the operands look numeric, since MySQL uses CONCAT() for string concatenation
MySQL automatically translates + into CONCAT() with no code changes needed
It works identically to SQL Server with no differences
MySQL disables the + operator entirely for all data types
questions.explain: Standard MySQL syntax has no + operator for string concatenation; CONCAT() is the correct equivalent.

questions.q: How does MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT differ structurally from how identity generation sometimes works in Oracle or PostgreSQL?
options: AUTO_INCREMENT is a property of the table itself with no separate sequence object involved
AUTO_INCREMENT requires creating and managing a separate SEQUENCE object
AUTO_INCREMENT can be applied to multiple columns per table simultaneously
AUTO_INCREMENT only works on non-key columns
questions.explain: Unlike Oracle's sequence-based approaches, MySQL's auto-increment counter is tracked internally by the storage engine as a table property.

questions.q: According to this lesson, is it accurate to assume every modern MySQL target loosely handles invalid data the way older MySQL versions did?
options: No — strict SQL mode has been the default since MySQL 5.7, so the sql_mode setting should be verified rather than assumed
Yes — all MySQL versions, past and present, silently coerce invalid data with no exceptions
No — MySQL has never had loose data handling at any point in its history
Yes — strict mode was removed from MySQL entirely in recent versions
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly corrects the outdated reputation: strict mode is the modern default, but the actual server setting still needs to be confirmed.

questions.q: What two capabilities does a table silently lose if it ends up running on the MyISAM storage engine instead of InnoDB?
options: Transaction support and row-level locking
The ability to store string data and the ability to use AUTO_INCREMENT
The ability to be queried with SELECT and the ability to have a primary key
Backup support and replication support entirely
questions.explain: MyISAM has no transaction support at all and locks at the table level rather than the row level, unlike InnoDB.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend explicitly specifying ENGINE=InnoDB when migrating tables to MySQL?
options: To ensure transactional integrity and row-level locking are actually preserved, rather than trusting a default that could land a table on a different engine
Because InnoDB is required for MySQL to support the CREATE TABLE statement at all
Because AUTO_INCREMENT only functions on the InnoDB engine
Because MyISAM has been completely removed from all current MySQL versions
questions.explain: Relying on an assumed default risks a table silently landing on a non-transactional, table-locking engine like MyISAM.
